extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students of literary criticism / Indian aesthetics / drama
extracted.subtask_description: A concise teaching/summary of the classical Indian 'Rasa' theory (from Bharata and later Sanskrit critics) explaining what Rasa is, how it is realized in drama, its features, the components (vibhava, anubhava, vyabhicaribhava), the eight sthayibhavas & rasas, abhinaya types, and rival scholarly accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary goal of dramatic performance
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary goal of drama is not mere entertainment but to create a 'parallel life' before the audience so they experience a sense of their own consciousness and engage with spiritual and moral questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic enactment should aim to evoke deeper self-reflection and ethical/spiritual resonance in the spectator rather than only amusement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drama as synthesis of the arts
rubrics_metrics.description: Drama is the synthesis of all arts and is the most perfect fruition of aesthetic activity (Bharata muni).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective drama integrates poetry, music, and action to achieve aesthetic fulfillment; staging should harmonize these elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Rasa (aesthetic pleasure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rasa signifies the aesthetic pleasure or thrill invariably accompanied by joy that the audience experiences while witnessing skilful enactment of a play 'rendered highly appealing through excellent poetry, music and action'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rasa is an experiential, felt quality in the spectator; performances should be crafted to produce this aesthetic relish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bharata's rasa sutra (source of Rasa)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rasa results from the union of Vibhavas, Anubhavas and Vyabhicharibhavas: 'Vibhavanubhava vyabhichari samyogat rasa nishpattihi'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To produce rasa, ensure the presence and interplay of causes (vibhava), effects/expressions (anubhava), and transitory states (vyabhicharibhava).

rubrics_metrics.name: Vibhava (causes/stimuli)
rubrics_metrics.description: Vibhava is the objective condition producing an emotion; it acts as a stimulus responsible for awakening sthayi (the permanent emotion). Vibhavas have two aspects: alambana (the person in whose mind sthayibhavas run) and uddipana (stimuli—e.g., moonlight, spring, soft breeze, fragrance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When crafting scenes, include clear situational causes and both relationship-centered (alambana) and environmental (uddipana) stimuli to evoke the intended sthayi.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anubhava (consequences/expressive effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Anubhavas are the physical changes and consequents seen in the character after emotions arise—expressed through words, gestures and facial expressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performers should manifest emotions through concrete anubhavas (speech, gesture, expression) so spectators can feel/experience abhinaya.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vyabhicharibhavas (transitory states)
rubrics_metrics.description: Vyabhicharibhavas (also sancharibhavas) are transitory or temporary mental states (thirty-three in number) that arise from the principal emotion and ultimately merge into it; examples include weakness, depression, anxiety, despair.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use transient affective shades to texture and transition toward the dominant sthayi; these are like waves that appear and disappear and give motion to the dominant emotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sthayibhavas produce dominant Rasas
rubrics_metrics.description: There are eight permanent instincts (sthayibhavas) inborn in humans; these produce the eight corresponding rasas (dominant permanent emotions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and sustain the appropriate sthayibhava in a work to cultivate the intended rasa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mapping of Sthayibhavas to Rasas
rubrics_metrics.description: Sthayibhavas & Rasas mapping: 1. Rati (love) → Shringara (erotic); 2. Hasa (laughter) → Hasya (comic); 3. Shoka (sorrow) → Karuna (pathetic/compassionate); 4. Krodha (anger) → Raudra (furious); 5. Utsaha (enthusiasm) → Vira (heroic); 6. Bhaya (fear) → Bhayanaka (terrifying); 7. Jugupsa (disgust) → Bibhatsa (disgusting); 8. Vismaya (wonder) → Adbhuta (wonderful/awesome).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing character psychology and plot, align stimuli, expressions and transient states to the chosen sthayibhava to yield the corresponding rasa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abhinaya types (modes of presentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rasas are presented through three kinds of dramatic representation or abhinaya: angik (that which uses the body), vachik (that which uses speech), and sattvik (involuntary/psychic expressions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A complete performance employs angik, vachik and sattvik abhinaya—bodily gesture, verbal expression, and subtle involuntary signs—to communicate bhavas and produce rasa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rasa as undefinable realization with detachment
rubrics_metrics.description: Rasa is an undefinable realization and intense feeling accompanied by detachment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rasa involves a felt intensity plus a distanced, aesthetic savoring rather than raw personal involvement; aim for controlled intensity that invites aesthetic relish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rasa as 'flavor' or 'essence' beyond the senses
rubrics_metrics.description: Rasa (literally 'flavour' or 'essence') implies something that cannot be captured directly by the senses; it is an abstract aesthetic sense retained from earlier concrete usages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat rasa as an emergent quality of poetic/dramatic composition—not reducible to single sensory inputs but to their integrated effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rasa is the soul of poetry/drama
rubrics_metrics.description: Bharata calls rasa the soul of poetry; without rasa there cannot be drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measures of literary/dramatic success should foreground whether a work achieves rasa—the central evaluative standard in this aesthetic tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rasa distinct from ordinary experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Rasa is not experienced in common situations but only in the art form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The aesthetic distance and formal devices of art are necessary conditions for rasa; ordinary emotion does not automatically yield aesthetic relish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rasa as pleasure experienced by different classes
rubrics_metrics.description: Rasa is the pleasure experienced by each class of people (i.e., different spectators may relish the aesthetic emotion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider audience-sensitivity: works may evoke rasas differently across spectators but still aim to produce an identifiable aesthetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rasa cannot be fully defined by words
rubrics_metrics.description: No other word can define rasa completely; it is an impression created on the mind of the sympathetic audience by expressions of bhavas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism should acknowledge the elusive, experiential quality of rasa while analyzing the mechanisms that produce it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rasa is experienced via depiction of Bhavas
rubrics_metrics.description: Rasa is the impression created on the mind of the sympathetic audience by the expressions of Bhavas (emotions) and is experienced by it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical focus should be on how bhavas are depicted—through situation (vibhava), expression (anubhava), and transitory states (vyabhicharibhava)—to create rasa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bhatt Lollata — uttpatti-upchiti vaad
rubrics_metrics.description: Bhatt Lollata's theory: rasa is produced due to vibhava; vibhava brings the sthayibhava out which is underlying in the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A productionist or critic following this view would emphasise constructing strong situational causes to elicit underlying emotions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sri Shankuka — anukruti-anumiti vaad (chitraturag nyay)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shankuka's theory: rasa's effect on the spectator comes through their involvement in the action; using the painted-horse analogy (chitraturag nyay), aesthetic experience is both neither wholly real nor unreal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on spectator involvement and imaginative identification; presentational illusion rather than literal reality is central to producing rasa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bhatt Nayak — Bhukti vaad
rubrics_metrics.description: Bhatt Nayak's theory: rasa is neither produced nor created; it cannot be measured and can only be enjoyed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This view treats rasa as an irreducible enjoyment; criticism may therefore be descriptive of experience rather than prescriptive about mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abhinavagupta — Abhivyakti vaad (transmission model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Abhinavagupta's theory: rasa is experienced first by the writer and then transmitted to the audience; natya-rasa is 'alaukik' or transcendental (from Abhinavabharati).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize authorial realization and skilled expression as prerequisites for transmitting rasa; consider textual/aesthetic strategies that enable transmission from creator to spectator.
